slides.0.title: Making white and rosé wine
slides.0.subtitle: Protect the fruit, or build texture? Every step is a choice
slides.1.title: From grapes to juice
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Hand and machine harvesting
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Hand picking allows selection and keeps whole bunches (needed for whole-bunch pressing and traditional-method sparkling); machine harvesting is fast and cheap and can work cool at night, but breaks berries
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Skin contact and whole-bunch pressing
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Brief skin contact before pressing adds aroma and texture (common for aromatic varieties) but also phenolics and bitterness; whole-bunch pressing gives clean, low-phenolic juice for delicate styles
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Settling (débourbage)
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Letting juice settle before fermentation removes solids; the cleaner the juice, the purer the fruit, though leaving some solids adds complexity and yeast nutrients
slides.1.content: White winemaking is about controlling oxygen and phenolics: the more fruit you want, the cooler, faster and less contact you need.
slides.2.title: Fermentation, MLF and maturation
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Fermentation temperature and yeast
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Whites usually ferment at about 12–22°C: cooler keeps esters and fruit, warmer adds texture; cultured yeasts are reliable and controllable, wild yeasts may add complexity but are riskier
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Malolactic conversion (MLF)
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Lactic bacteria convert sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, lowering acidity, adding roundness and possibly buttery diacetyl. Common in high-acid cool regions; usually blocked for fresh aromatic whites
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Oak and lees
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Barrel fermentation or ageing brings vanilla, toast and the texture of micro-oxygenation; lees stirring (bâtonnage) adds creamy, bready notes and roundness. Stainless steel keeps pure fruit
slides.2.content: One Chardonnay can span the full range from crisp to rich through MLF, oak and lees.
slides.3.title: Four ways to make rosé
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Direct pressing
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Red grapes pressed straight away with minimal skin contact: the palest, most delicate style, typical of Provence
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Short maceration
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Juice and skins macerate for a few hours to a day or two before separation, giving deeper colour and flavour (e.g. Tavel, some Bandol)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Saignée
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Some juice is bled from a red-wine vat to make rosé while concentrating the remaining red; the rosé is a by-product, deeper and fuller in style
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Blending red and white
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Adding red wine to white. The EU in principle does not allow this for still rosé; rosé Champagne is the best-known exception
slides.3.content: A rosé’s colour is a result of winemaking choices, not a guarantee of quality.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What does malolactic conversion mainly change?
A. Converts sugar to alcohol
B. Adds tannin
C. Removes pigment
D. Converts malic to lactic acid, lowering acidity
MLF can also bring buttery diacetyl.
To keep the fresh fruit of an aromatic white, what is usually done?
A. Ferment warm and do MLF
B. Ferment cool, block MLF, use stainless steel
C. Long ageing in new oak
D. Weeks of extended skin contact
Cool temperatures and minimal contact keep esters and primary fruit.
Which rosé method usually gives the palest colour?
A. Long maceration
B. Direct pressing
C. Saignée
D. Short maceration
Direct pressing has the shortest skin contact.
What is the best-known EU exception allowing rosé by blending red and white?
A. Côtes de Provence
B. Rioja Rosado
C. Tavel
D. Rosé Champagne
Blending is not allowed in principle for still rosé.
